Centralized Error Handling

Why every error funnels through one file, instead of a try/catch in every controller.

Without any of this project's pattern, a natural instinct is to handle errors right where they can occur:

// The alternative this project deliberately avoids:
export const getTicketById = async (req, res) => {
  try {
    const ticket = await ticketService.getTicketById(Number(req.params.id));
    if (!ticket) return res.status(404).json({ error: { message: 'Not found' } });
    res.json(ticket);
  } catch (err) {
    res.status(500).json({ error: { message: 'Internal Server Error' } });
  }
};

That works for one controller — but repeat it across every controller this API will ever have, and the response shape for an error ({ error: { message } }) is now duplicated everywhere, with every future contributor free to format it slightly differently by hand.

This project's approach, now that all three pieces are in view, is the opposite: no controller ever handles its own errors. Instead:

  1. asyncHandler (Figure 1.9) catches a rejected Promise from any controller and calls next(err).
  2. Express routes that straight to errorHandler (Figure 1.10) — skipping every ordinary middleware in between — because of its four-argument signature.
  3. errorHandler, registered last in app.js (Figure 1.3, first topic), is the one and only place an error becomes a JSON response.

That's also precisely why app.js registers errorHandler dead last: it has to sit downstream of every route and every other middleware for next(err) to be able to reach it from anywhere in the app. Add a hundred more routes later, and none of them need their own try/catch — they just need to be wrapped in asyncHandler, and any error they throw ends up here automatically.
